exp_pool.title: Is Watching Porn Cheating in a Relationship?
exp_pool.text: You found porn on your partner’s phone, and now you’re wondering if watching porn is cheating or if you’re overreacting. Or maybe you’re the one whose partner found it, and you genuinely don’t understand why something you never considered cheating suddenly feels like betrayal to them. Either way, you can end up arguing about a question neither of you ever actually said out loud. That’s why couples can so easily talk past each other when it comes to porn. One person is focused on the fact that no touching happened and no one else was in the room. The other is focused on sexual arousal happening outside the relationship and the fact that it was kept from them. When you’ve never talked about what porn means in your relationship, that silence can create a gap between what each of you thought you had agreed to. In this episode of The RISE to Intimacy Podcast, I break down three common myths about porn in relationships, including whether it counts as cheating, whether it harms relationships, and whether regular use means addiction. smm_pool.title: How much does YouTube pay per view in 2026?
smm_pool.text: Key takeaways YouTube pays per ad view, not per video view, typically an estimated $5 to $15 per 1,000 ad views in 2026. Your earnings per view depend on your content niche, audience location, ad type, video length, and seasonal advertiser demand. RPM (revenue per mille) shows what you actually earn after YouTube’s 45% cut, while CPM reflects what advertisers pay. Ad revenue is only one income stream. Brand deals, channel memberships, affiliate marketing, and merch can meaningfully increase total YouTube earnings. How YouTube’s pay-per-view system works YouTube does have a pay-per-view system , but it might not be what you’d initially think. Instead of getting paid for each video view, YouTubers are paid for each ad view. Let’s dig a little deeper into what these two types of views mean: Video views: The number of views your video gets. Ad views: The number of views that ads on your video get. YouTube pays you for the amount of ad views your video gets. If your video has a million views but no advertising on it, you won’t be making any money. If your video has a million views but only 10,000 ad views, you’ll be making money only on the 10,000 ad views. Similarly, you might have multiple ads run within a single YouTube video. If users actually watch those ads all the way through, you could also end up with more ad views than video views. Essentially, YouTube makes money off the advertising space, so it will only pay based on how much exposure your video generates for that advertising space. Of that advertising money, YouTube keeps 45% and you keep 55% . Through this model, YouTube has paid creators over $100 billion since 2021. The short version: Your YouTube income is a share of ad revenue tied to ad views, not a flat rate per video view. Bonus: Download the free 30-day plan to grow your YouTube following fast , a daily workbook of challenges that will help you kickstart your Youtube channel growth and track your success. Get real results after one month. What are CPM, RPM, and CPC on YouTube? CPM, RPM, and CPC are the three metrics that explain the gap between what advertisers spend and what lands in your bank account. They sound similar, but they measure very different things, and mixing them up is the fastest way to end up disappointed by your first payout. smm_pool.title: How to get verified on Instagram in 2026
smm_pool.text: What does Instagram verification mean? Instagram verification is the process of getting a blue checkmark badge that appears next to your username on the platform. The verification badge signals to other users on the platform that an account really belongs to the user, artist, brand, or organization it represents. If you’re looking to enhance your presence while pursuing verification, consider brainstorming unique Instagram username ideas that reflect your brand identity. Data storytelling is the practice of using facts, statistics, and quantitative information to build a compelling narrative that an audience can understand and act on. In other words, it uses real numbers to support an engaging story and authenticate the story’s message. “Using data to tell stories from a brand’s point of view can be very effective, as it bridges that place between logic and emotion and lets a brand connect with a reader on a deeper level,” says Leeann Froese, Digital Marketing Manager at Town Hall Brands. Data can “prove” the validity of a story (for example, sheep are smart: Research shows they can remember the visual identities of up to 50 individual faces ) and help sell a brand or product (Ie: When “four out of five dentists” recommend a specific toothpaste). That brings us to another important part of data storytelling: the numbers need to be true, unaltered, and preferably provided by a trusted third party. Making up numbers or bending statistics to suit your own needs is a dangerous game, especially on social media. Every good data story rests on three things working together: the data itself, the narrative around it, and the visuals that carry it. What are the three pillars of data storytelling? The three pillars of data storytelling are data, narrative, and visualization. Drop any one of them and the story falls flat: data alone is dry, narrative alone is unproven, and visuals alone are decoration. Data The foundation is accurate, relevant, and verifiable information. That might be third-party research, platform data, or your own first-party numbers from sales, surveys, or social analytics. Whatever the origin, it needs to come from trusted sources you can name publicly. If you cannot point to where a number came from, it does not belong in the story. Loyal customers cost less to retain than new ones cost to acquire, spend more over time, and actively recommend the brand to others. Building brand loyalty in 2026 requires consistent experiences, personalized engagement, fast customer care, and smart use of AI to anticipate customer needs. Key metrics for tracking brand loyalty include net promoter score, customer lifetime value, engagement rate, and sentiment analysis. What is brand loyalty? Brand loyalty is the connection between a brand and a customer that drives someone to make repeat purchases from a specific brand. They stick with that brand even when alternative suppliers or products may be cheaper or more easily accessible. The lineup outside the Apple Store to get the latest iPhone the first morning it’s available? That’s brand loyalty in action. What separates loyalty from habit is the emotional connection behind the purchase. A habitual buyer picks your product because it’s there. A loyal customer picks it because it says something about who they are, and because they trust you to deliver. That trust is built over time through familiarity with your brand (also known as brand awareness ), satisfying early experiences, and consistency after the sale. smm_pool.text: LinkedIn is still one of the best places to build an audience from scratch, and you can increase your LinkedIn followers there organically, with no paid ads, no follower buying, and no growth hacks. When I went through 52 million posts across 10 platforms for our State of Social Media Engagement report , LinkedIn had the highest median engagement rate of any platform we looked at, at around 6.2%. LinkedIn has also become the most-cited website in AI search for professional questions, according to Profound's tracking, and more of what gets cited is what people post. So what you share on LinkedIn can show up when someone asks ChatGPT about your field. It's worked for me, too. I made my account in 2017 but only started posting in 2020 , when I was looking for community after losing my job. I now have over 25,000 followers, and posting has led to brand partnerships and invites onto podcasts and YouTube channels, which I never would've thought possible when I started. You don't need millions of followers, and you don't need to be the world's foremost expert in your niche. A smaller following that cares about what you have to say will do far more for you than a huge one that doesn't. So if you really, really want to grow on LinkedIn, whether as a creator, a founder, a business owner, or someone starting from zero, this guide is for you. It pairs what's worked for me with Buffer's data on millions of LinkedIn posts, and there's a section for company pages too. Key takeaways Switch your profile's main button from Connect to Follow. Connections are capped at 30,000 and need a yes from both sides, while followers have no cap, and everyone who connects with you follows you anyway. Stick to three to five topics. LinkedIn's feed now matches posts to people based on what they're about, so a clear focus helps it find your audience. Try carousels. In Buffer's analysis of 52 million posts, LinkedIn carousels had a median engagement rate of 21.77%, about three times video and nearly seven times text-only posts. Don't worry about posting too often. In Buffer's study of 2 million+ LinkedIn posts, accounts posting 11 or more times a week averaged nearly 17,000 more impressions per post. Reply to your comments. About 83% of LinkedIn profiles in Buffer's data performed better when they replied, the highest share of any platform. Keep your posts sounding like you. LinkedIn added a "Seems like AI slop" report option in July 2026, and flagged posts are seeing about 40% fewer views.
